I think beginning maybe a meeting in August, we began to have conversation regarding a mandate from SED, the State Education Department pertaining to districts that were participating in the Race to the Top program. This initiative required all participating school districts to select a data dashboard, which was going to be provided free of charge to school districts for two years, and after the two-year period had expired, the districts would bear the cost of those particular services. There were a number of concerns that began to surface, not only from Irvington, from our leadership team, but also from districts and parent groups across the entire state. But first locally we had concerns about this being a non-funded mandate, and that as we move forward with this initiative the district would have to bear all of the costs for this where a number of the services associated with this database were included a parent portal, and the parent portal would provide students and their parents with access to grades and other achievement data that's similar to what we currently provide in our own portal, which they can access. There was also concerns about our ability to not only meet the financial needs associated with this because it's certainly not the cost of the fees associated with the service, but it is the man hours, the human resource time that would go into managing this type of initiative. So it posed a tremendous concern for us on that front, and many of our neighboring districts shared that same worry. But there was also a larger growing concern about the privacy of student data. SED contracted with a not-for-profit organization that received its funding originally from the Gates Foundation for this type of purpose, to provide clearinghouse data for school districts. Its original intent, as was marketed by a number of different groups, including in Bloom, was to provide more access to not only educators but to parents with a target on communities where this information was not being shared. But there's a lot of concern with respect to that data that is being shared. There are over approximately 400 data points that would be uploaded for each and every child. ranging from obvious things of some student identifiers and student grades to scores on achievement tests, but also other data that pertain to their economic status, their race, students' gender, of course. And one that was really outside of the box of normal reporting that we would see with SED or other agencies was whether students identified with a non-traditional sexual orientation or gender type, which was very peculiar because you've got to begin to wonder why does SED need that information and why are we at liberty to share that information. Certainly SED holds the rights to some student information as it pertains to their achievement data on state tests, regents exams, and so forth. But I hold that the district and families hold the responsibility of protecting the rest of that data, and that we should take every effort possible to ensure that we're not sharing information that our families didn't intend to be shared with this outside organization.
